                    ### Question
                    A 16-year-old male is brought to the clinic by his mother for the complaints of fever, nonproductive cough, fatigue, lack of appetite, and sore throat for the past 2 months.  Several other students at his high school have had similar symptoms. Physical exam shows a whitish membrane in his oropharynx, bilateral enlarged cervical lymphadenopathy, and mild splenomegaly.  Which of the following tests is most likely to diagnose his condition.?

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The symptoms of fever, nonproductive cough, fatigue, lack of appetite, sore throat, whitish membrane in the oropharynx, bilateral enlarged cervical lymphadenopathy, and mild splenomegaly in a 16-year-old male suggest infectious mononucleosis, commonly caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). The Monospot test is a heterophile antibody test used to diagnose infectious mononucleosis and is the most appropriate diagnostic test in this scenario. The reasoning chains supporting the Monospot test align with the standard medical consensus for diagnosing EBV-related infectious mononucleosis. The retrieved evidence paths related to enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) are not directly relevant to diagnosing infectious mononucleosis in this context, as ELISA is not typically used for this purpose. Therefore, the Monospot test is the most likely to diagnose the condition accurately.
